--- title: "Types of learning" description: "Some data come with answers and some do not. Supervised learning predicts a known answer; unsupervised learning looks for groups. A short example of each on one coastal survey, which the rest of the course also uses." order: 1 categories: [foundations, supervised, unsupervised] --- ## The data decide the kind of learning Machine learning comes with a long list of names: regression, classification, clustering, random forests, neural networks. They are easier to hold on to once you can place them on a map. The first division on that map depends on the data you hold rather than the method you choose. **Supervised learning** learns from examples with a known answer. Each example has measurements and an outcome, and the model learns to get from one to the other. The outcome sets the task: *regression* when it is a quantity, such as a temperature, and *classification* when it is a category, such as "yes" or "no". **Unsupervised learning** has no outcome at all. It receives a table of measurements and looks for structure in it: groups of similar examples, or variables that move together. Nothing tells it which answer is right, so its results need extra care. A third kind, **reinforcement learning**, learns from the consequences of its own actions: an autonomous underwater vehicle might learn a sampling route by trial, rewarded for each useful measurement. It needs a way to act and a reward, not a table of data, and this course does not cover it. ::: {.diagram} ![Three kinds of learning. Supervised learning has an answer for every example; unsupervised learning has none and looks for groups; reinforcement learning acts, receives a reward, and adjusts. The table shows the first five stations of the survey.](img/learning-types.svg){fig-alt="Three panels. The supervised panel shows a table of five stations with columns for temperature, salinity and depth, and a highlighted answer column, found, reading yes, no, no, yes, yes. The unsupervised panel shows grey points by temperature and depth, falling into three dashed circles. The reinforcement panel shows a box for an underwater vehicle above a box for the sea, joined in a loop: an arrow labelled action, move and sample, runs down to the sea, and an arrow labelled reward and new position runs back up."} ::: ## One coastal survey runs through the course Every example in this course uses the same dataset: a survey of 800 stations on a temperate coastal shelf, visited between 2018 and 2023. At each station the survey measured the water and counted one species of seabed animal. This page uses five of its columns: - **temperature**, the water temperature, in °C; - **salinity**, in practical salinity units (PSU), close to grams of salt per kilogram of seawater; - **depth**, in metres; - **abundance**, the number of animals counted at the station; - **present**, "yes" if at least one animal was found, "no" otherwise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() survey |> select(station_id, temperature_c, salinity_psu, depth_m, abundance, present) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station_id | temperature_c| salinity_psu| depth_m| abundance|present | |:----------|-------------:|------------:|-------:|---------:|:-------| |ST0001 | 11.15| 33.26| 99.2| 15|yes | |ST0002 | 4.42| 34.20| 134.7| 0|no | |ST0003 | 14.69| 33.67| 52.3| 0|no | |ST0004 | 10.02| 33.47| 90.8| 21|yes | |ST0005 | 6.35| 34.22| 125.0| 1|yes |
::: ::: The survey is simulated: we wrote the program that generated it, so we know the true relationships and can check whether a model finds them. It records more columns than these five. [Section 2](../02-marine-data/index.qmd) introduces the full dataset and the work needed before modelling it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Supervised learning on the survey Three quarters of the stations are kept for fitting and a quarter set aside for later pages. Three new stations, one shallow, one mid-depth and one deep, serve as the test case every model is asked about. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = present) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) new_stations <- tibble( station = c("shallow", "mid-depth", "deep"), temperature_c = c(12, 9, 5), salinity_psu = c(33.4, 33.7, 34.2), depth_m = c(40, 90, 150) ) ``` ::: These three stations are made up for illustration; they are not part of the survey. The names shallow, mid-depth and deep are labels we gave them from their depths (40, 90 and 150 m) so the text can refer to them. The models never see the names, only the three measurements. ### Classification: is the species present? With presence as the outcome, the task is a classification. **Logistic regression** is linear regression adapted to a yes-or-no outcome, so that its answer is a probability between 0 and 1. A squared temperature term lets that probability rise and then fall again. [Section 3](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) covers it in full. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classifier <- logistic_reg() |> fit(present ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:---------|---------:|---------:| |shallow | 0.8516393| 0.1483607| |mid-depth | 0.8928048| 0.1071952| |deep | 0.5163755| 0.4836245|
::: ::: For each new station the model returns the chance that the species is present, and the chance that it is not. ### Regression: how many animals? Change the outcome to the number of animals counted and the same survey becomes a *regression* problem. An ordinary linear regression: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regression <- linear_reg() |> fit(abundance ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) tidy(regression) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------|----------:|----------:|----------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 21.6048715| 25.9757817| 0.8317313| 0.4058937| |temperature_c | -0.0838936| 0.0765104| -1.0964989| 0.2733033| |salinity_psu | -0.4286569| 0.7821813| -0.5480275| 0.5838782| |depth_m | -0.0282825| 0.0071275| -3.9680934| 0.0000813|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(regression, new_stations)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred| |:---------|--------:| |shallow | 5.149706| |mid-depth | 3.858663| |deep | 2.282957|
::: ::: Abundance falls with depth, by about 0.03 animals per metre. Salinity has no clear effect, which is correct: we built none into the simulation. The temperature slope is close to zero, even though the classification needed a curved temperature term. [The next page](what-is-machine-learning.qmd) takes up that puzzle. ## Unsupervised learning on the survey Now remove the answers entirely: no abundance, no presence, only temperature, salinity and depth. We ask **k-means clustering** to sort the 800 stations into three groups. It works in four steps: 1. Place three group centres among the stations, at random. 2. Assign every station to its nearest centre. 3. Move each centre to the average of the stations assigned to it. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until no station changes group. "Nearest" is measured across all three variables at once, so they must be on a common scale first. Depth spans nearly 200 metres and salinity about two units; without rescaling, depth alone would decide every group. [Section 2](../02-marine-data/index.qmd) returns to this. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) clusters <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = 3) |> set_engine("stats")) |> fit(survey) clustered <- bind_cols(survey, extract_cluster_assignment(clusters)) clustered |> summarise( stations = n(), `depth (m)` = round(mean(depth_m)), `temp (°C)` = round(mean(temperature_c), 1), `salinity (PSU)` = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2), .by = .cluster ) |> arrange(`depth (m)`) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | stations| depth (m)| temp (°C)| salinity (PSU)| |:---------|--------:|---------:|---------:|--------------:| |Cluster_1 | 241| 45| 10.5| 33.36| |Cluster_3 | 296| 89| 9.2| 33.74| |Cluster_2 | 263| 133| 6.3| 34.07|
::: ::: The three groups follow depth: shallow and warm, mid-depth, and deep and cold. That is no surprise, because in this survey the three variables move together: salinity rises with depth, and temperature falls with it. The cluster numbers themselves mean nothing; k-means numbers its groups in whatever order it happens to find them. ## Supervised and unsupervised compared Ask both kinds of model about the three new stations. The supervised classifier gives a chance of presence; k-means gives a group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_cols( select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob") |> select(.pred_yes), predict(clusters, new_stations) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes|.pred_cluster | |:---------|---------:|:-------------| |shallow | 0.8516393|Cluster_1 | |mid-depth | 0.8928048|Cluster_3 | |deep | 0.5163755|Cluster_2 |
::: ::: The classifier's answer is about the species, because the species was its target. k-means returns only a number, `Cluster_1` to `Cluster_3`, which says nothing on its own. To give the groups names, the code below sorts them by the average depth of their stations, 45, 89 and 133 m in the table above, and calls them Shallow, Mid-depth and Deep. The names are ours; k-means knows only the numbers. With names attached, the groups can be compared with something k-means never saw: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Name each cluster after the average depth of its stations. depth_order <- clustered |> summarise(depth = mean(depth_m), .by = .cluster) |> arrange(depth) |> mutate(group = c("Shallow", "Mid-depth", "Deep")) clustered <- clustered |> left_join(select(depth_order, .cluster, group), by = ".cluster") |> mutate(group = factor(group, levels = depth_order$group)) clustered |> summarise(stations = n(), `species present` = round(mean(present == "yes"), 2), `mean abundance` = round(mean(abundance), 2), .by = group) |> arrange(group) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|group | stations| species present| mean abundance| |:---------|--------:|---------------:|--------------:| |Shallow | 241| 0.81| 4.94| |Mid-depth | 296| 0.82| 4.26| |Deep | 263| 0.69| 2.52|
::: ::: The species turns up at about four in five shallow and mid-depth stations, and at 69% of deep ones, where the average catch is half that of the shallow group (@fig-clusters). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_space <- ggplot(clustered, aes(depth_m, temperature_c, colour = group)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL, title = "The groups k-means found") p_abund <- ggplot(clustered, aes(group, abundance, fill = group)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) + guides(fill = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Abundance", title = "Abundance in each group", subtitle = "k-means did not use abundance") p_space + p_abund + plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: stations by depth and temperature, coloured by the group k-means assigned. Right: abundance in each group. The clustering never saw abundance, yet the shallow group holds about twice as many animals as the deep one.](types-of-learning_files/figure-html/fig-clusters-1.png){#fig-clusters fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a scatter plot of temperature against depth, with points coloured into three groups that mostly follow depth, with some overlap: shallow and warm on the left, mid-depth in the middle, deep and cold on the right. The right panel is a boxplot of abundance for each group; the shallow group has the highest median and the deep group the lowest.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Supervised | Unsupervised | | --- | --- | --- | | Needs | An answer for every training station | Only the measurements | | Returns | A prediction of the answer | A group, with no meaning attached | | Can be checked | Against stations held back, whose answers are known | Only indirectly, against things it never saw | | Example here | The chance of presence | Shallow, mid-depth and deep groups | So the groups do differ in the species, although k-means never saw a single catch. This is unsupervised learning at its most useful and its most tempting. Ask for six groups and you get six, each just as confidently defined. [Section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) covers the checks that tell a real structure from an artefact of the method. ## Labels and groups both need care **Unsupervised does not mean assumption-free.** Choosing k-means, choosing three groups, choosing the variables and their scaling: each is a modelling decision, and each shapes the groups. **Labels are often less solid than they look.** Two specialists classifying the same seabed images disagree more often than most people expect. A supervised model can never be more reliable than the labels it learned from. **The boundaries blur in practice.** Semi-supervised learning combines a few labels with many unlabelled examples; self-supervised learning builds labels from the data's own structure. The division on this page is a teaching map, not a law. [Discriminative and generative models](discriminative-and-generative-models.qmd) adds a second division, by the thing the model learns. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Supervised learning needs examples with known answers. Regression predicts a quantity, classification a category. - Unsupervised learning has no answers. Methods such as k-means find groups, and will always return as many as you ask for. - Reinforcement learning learns from the consequences of actions, and is outside this course. - A supervised model is no more reliable than its labels; an unsupervised one is shaped by the choices made in setting it up. ::: ## Try it yourself Refit the clustering with `num_clusters = 6`, then with `num_clusters = 2`. Do the groups still look like real habitats? Which evidence would make you prefer one answer over another?
